fetched_contents.text: Gaps in Reporting Greenhouse Gas Emissions by German Hospitals—A Systematic Grey Literature Review 1. Introduction Climate change is posing threats to human health, for instance, through increased mortality in extreme weather events or by decreasing agricultural yields and rising sea levels, endangering human livelihoods [1]. However, in the climate change discourse, health and the health sector have more nuanced roles than that. The health sector, including “all organizations, institutions and resources devoted to producing health actions” [1], will not only be impacted by climate change, but will also be key in adapting to climate change and to motivate climate-friendly behaviour [2,3]. At the same time, the health sector is also a relevant contributor to rising levels of GHG emissions and thereby to climate change. In Germany, the health sector is responsible for 6.7% (55.1 Mt CO2) of the country’s GHG emissions [4]. One third of the GHG emissions are energy-related [5]: either direct from sources owned or controlled by healthcare facilities (Scope 1) or indirect from purchased electricity, steam, heating and cooling consumed by the healthcare facilities (Scope 2). Two-thirds of the GHG emissions are produced up- and downstream of health facilities, e.g., along supply chains and disposal of medical equipment and pharmaceuticals (Scope 3). Ambitious targets for climate change mitigation exist. On the international level, the Paris Agreement, which entered into force in 2016, aims at keeping the global average temperature increase below 2 °C and pursing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels [6]. On the European level, the European Green Deal endeavors to achieve a climate neutral European Union by 2050 [7]. On the national level, the Klimaschutzgesetz (Federal Climate Change Act) passed by the German Federal Government in 2019, commits to a 55% reduction in GHG emissions by 2030 compared to the 1990 levels [8]. To meet the targets on international, European and national level, all sectors, including the health sector, need to undergo changes. Such changes will need to be radical in nature and therefore have been referred to in Germany as “Große Transformation,” a societal transformation towards sustainability [9]. Moreover, the fundamental maxim in medical ethics—“first, do no harm”—is violated by exceeding the unavoidable contribution to climate change as this negatively affects human health [10]. Especially German hospitals have to cut their GHG emissions as they are energy- and resource-intensive [11]. An Austrian study showed that hospitals are responsible for about one-third of the GHG emissions of the Austrian health sector [12]. In Germany, no such numbers exist, yet hospitals account for about 25% of German healthcare spending [13], which gives an idea about the share of GHG emissions, as financial indicators such as GDP correlate with GHG emissions [14]. To begin the transition to low-carbon hospitals, an EU-funded project formulated a list of “Simple Steps to Reduce the Climate Impact of Healthcare.” The steps are (1) mapping the GHG emissions of hospitals, (2) identifying emission sources with the greatest impact, (3) working with measures to reduce the impact and (4) evaluating the results [15]. Consequently, before being able to reduce GHG emissions of German hospitals, it is vital to perform step 1 and 2. In order to map the GHG emissions (step 1) and identify GHG emission sources with greatest impacts (step 2), it is important to see how many German hospitals do report on their GHG emissions and to examine characteristics of the reports with regard to comprehensiveness and assessed GHG emissions sources. As peer-reviewed literature did not provide the required information, a systematic grey literature review was performed. The search strategy included hand-searching specific databases and websites and using web search engines. To validate this strategy, websites of all hospitals in the federal state of Saarland were hand-searched. This review identified severe gaps in the current status of GHG emissions reports of German hospitals. Only few German hospitals report their GHG emissions focusing on low-hanging fruits which account for a small fraction of the actual GHG emissions of the hospital. To meet GHG reduction targets, German hospitals should be obliged to follow a standardized methodology to report and reduce their GHG emissions. 2. fetched_contents.text: Measuring greenhouse gas emissions in health systems 22 December 2025 | Publication Overview Climate change is a growing health crisis, driving increased mortality from heat, malnutrition, and disease, and placing increasing pressure on health systems worldwide. Despite the Paris Agreement goal of limiting long-run warming to 1.5 °C, global temperatures have already exceeded this threshold over the course of a single year. The health sector contributes to approximately 5% of global emissions. It is imperative that health systems rapidly prepare for further increases in global temperatures, while also reducing their own carbon footprints. Measurement of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is central to credible decarbonization planning over the long term. It enables target-setting, identification of emissions hotspots, design of interventions, public accountability, and tracking of progress over time. Without GHG emissions measurement, action risks being misdirected, unaccountable, ineffective or insufficient to meet national and global climate targets. This document has two aims. First, it defines a common approach for health system emissions measurement that is aligned with international standards and best practice. Second, it sets out how health systems can develop the necessary internal capabilities to measure their emissions consistently and effectively over time. Editors World Health Organization

fetched_contents.text: Emergent climate protection strategies in German hospitals: A cluster analysis * Loading metrics Open Access Peer-reviewed Research Article * Sabine Bohnet-Joschko Emergent climate protection strategies in German hospitals: A cluster analysis * Lara Schmidt, * Sabine Bohnet-Joschko x * Published: May 16, 2025 * https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0312661 Figures Abstract Hospitals emit large amounts of greenhouse gas emissions during healthcare delivery due to their extensive resource utilization and substantial waste generation. By implementing climate actions, hospitals can significantly contribute to climate protection in healthcare. This paper delves into the climate protection efforts of German hospitals, with a specific focus on the emergent strategies of hospital administrative leaders and the employee engagement within the framework of Stakeholder Theory. The investigation is based on primary data from an online survey of hospital administrative leaders in German hospitals. Employing a hierarchical cluster analysis, the study identifies four distinct clusters of hospitals. These clusters vary significantly in their organization and communication strategies regarding climate protection and allocation of responsibilities, indicating that German hospitals prioritize climate protection to varying degrees. The findings suggest that employee engagement depends on how hospital administrative leaders organize and communicate the topic of climate protection in their institutions. The study underscores the importance of strategic leadership for climate protection in hospitals. The evidence indicates that German hospital ownership is not governed by a single, unified legal definition across all sources, but several sources do distinguish broad categories. One source states that the term “nonprofit organizations” is not legally defined in Germany, though it is often used in various fields of science [N1-R5]. Another source says that “charity” in Germany is a tax-law concept, not a separate body of law [N1-R2]. A hospital-sector source reports that German hospitals are either publicly owned and run by local or federal state authorities (28.8%), owned by private for-profit organizations (37.1%), or otherwise categorized, suggesting a more granular ownership typology exists in practice [N1-R4]. A related healthcare privatization paper also analyzes public and charitable hospitals, implying that charitable hospitals are a distinct category within the sector [N1-R3].

The distinction between public, private, non-profit, and charitable hospitals is therefore partially definitional and partially operational. Public hospitals are explicitly described as state-owned or operated by local/federal authorities [N1-R4]. Private for-profit hospitals are clearly identified as a separate category in the ownership breakdown [N1-R4]. Charitable hospitals are treated as part of the sector in the privatization paper, but the evidence also notes that charity is defined mainly in tax law rather than in a separate body of law [N1-R2]. Non-profit hospitals are not directly defined in the provided evidence, but the broader nonprofit literature shows that the concept is often used in practice even if not legally formalized in a single German definition [N1-R5]. Non-profit status is not directly legally defined in the evidence provided, but it is present in the broader nonprofit literature and in hospital-sector datasets [N1-R5; N5-R3]. **The answer is not that ownership type explains a clear difference in reporting rates.** The evidence suggests instead that:

- German hospitals are classified into **public, private for-profit, charitable, and non-profit** categories, but the legal and operational definitions are not fully unified [N1-R2; N1-R4; N1-R5; N5-R3].
- **GHG emissions reporting is voluntary, not legally mandatory**, and overall coverage is low [N2-R2; N2-R5].

- **Data quality and methodology differ across hospitals**, and scope 3 emissions complicate reporting [N2-F1; N3-R3; N4-F2].
- **Generalizability is limited**, and the evidence is best interpreted as showing a weak overall status of reporting rather than a clear ownership pattern [N2-F1; N2-R5; N4-F2].

## Final conclusion

If you are asking whether public hospitals report more, private hospitals report less, or non-profit/charitable hospitals differ, the evidence does **not** support a clear answer. ## Integrated final answer: How do greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reporting rates vary among different hospital ownership types in Germany?

The available evidence suggests that **German hospitals report GHG emissions very little overall**, and the data are too limited to support a strong, consistent pattern by ownership type. In other words, the answer is not that ownership type explains a clear and statistically significant difference in reporting rates; rather, it is that reporting is generally low, with large methodological and institutional barriers, and ownership-type differences are not well established in the provided evidence [N2-R2; N2-R5; N2-F1].

### 1) What ownership types exist in German hospitals?

German hospital ownership is not governed by a single unified legal definition, but the evidence identifies several common categories used in hospital data: **public**, **private for-profit**, **charitable**, and **non-profit** hospitals [N1-R4; N1-R2; N1-R5; N5-R3]. 

- **Public hospitals** are explicitly described as hospitals owned and operated by local or federal state authorities [N1-R4].
- **Private for-profit hospitals** are clearly identified in the ownership breakdown as a separate category [N1-R4].
- **Charitable hospitals** are treated as part of the hospital sector, but the evidence notes that “charity” in Germany is a tax-law concept rather than a separate body of law [N1-R2; N1-R3].
- **Non-profit hospitals** are not directly legally defined in the evidence provided, but the broader nonprofit literature and hospital-sector datasets suggest that the category is used in practice [N1-R5; N5-R3].

In short, German hospital ownership is best understood as a mix of **public, private for-profit, charitable, and non-profit** categories, with charitable and non-profit status often defined through tax or institutional labels rather than a single statutory definition [N1-R2; N1-R5; N1-R4].

### 2) What reporting rules and incentives affect GHG emissions disclosure?

Reporting in Germany is **voluntary, not legally mandatory** for hospitals [N2-R2]. This is a key structural fact: hospitals are not required by law to report GHG emissions. 

At the same time, hospitals are under **strong climate-policy pressure**. The evidence notes ambitious climate targets at international, European, and national levels, including the Paris Agreement, the European Green Deal, and the German Federal Climate Change Act [N2-F1]. It also argues that hospitals should be obliged to follow a standardized methodology to report and reduce emissions if they are to meet these targets [N2-F1]. This implies that reporting is increasingly framed as a policy and institutional responsibility, not only an optional disclosure activity.

The incentives and barriers are therefore mixed:
- **Incentives** include policy pressure, climate targets, and the recognition that leadership and employee engagement matter for climate protection [N2-F1; N5-F3].
- **Barriers** include the lack of a legal obligation, limited reporting capacity, and methodological complexity [N2-R2; N2-F1].

The evidence also suggests that **reporting standards vary by hospital size and sector**. The 2020 data show that GHG emission reports were available for only 12% of German hospitals [N2-R5], and the systematic review found that reports tend to focus on low-hanging fruits, which account for only a small fraction of actual emissions [N2-F1]. Scope 3 emissions dominate, which are harder to measure and report than Scope 1 and 2 emissions [N2-F1; N3-R3]. A methodological study also shows that hospitals can calculate emissions using financial data from a P&L statement, but the evidence does not indicate that this approach is universally adopted [N6-R1]. The WHO guidance further states that health system emissions measurement must be aligned with international standards and best practice, but the evidence here shows that many hospitals do not have the necessary reporting infrastructure [N4-F2].

So the practical implication is: **strong policy pressure exists, but current reporting behavior remains weak, and the tools and standards needed for reliable disclosure are not evenly available** [N2-F1; N4-F2].

### 3) Evidence on observed differences in reporting rates by ownership type

The evidence available is **thin and mostly indirect**. The most direct finding is that, as of 2020, GHG emission reports were available for only **12% of German hospitals** [N2-R5]. Another source explicitly states that **no legal obligation for hospitals to report GHG emissions exists in Germany** [N2-R2]. A systematic grey literature review also found **severe gaps in the current status of GHG emissions reports** and noted that reports tend to focus on low-hanging fruits [N2-F1]. 

The evidence does **not** show a clear ownership-type pattern. It does not provide a direct comparison of reporting rates for public, private, non-profit, or charitable hospitals. The closest thing is the overall low reporting rate and the note that reports often focus on only a small fraction of actual emissions [N2-R5; N2-F1]. A related study on hospital GHG measurement shows that scope 3 emissions accounted for the majority of emissions in a German university hospital [N3-R3], but again, this does not compare ownership types.

Therefore, the conclusion is:
- **There is no strong evidence of a consistent ownership-type difference in reporting rates** [N2-R2; N2-R5; N2-F1].
- The evidence supports a conclusion of **low overall reporting**, not a clear pattern by ownership type [N2-R5; N2-F1].

### 4) Data quality, methodology, and comparability across ownership types

The evidence suggests that **data quality and measurement methodology differ across hospitals and across studies**, which makes comparisons by ownership type difficult [N2-F1; N2-R5; N3-R1; N6-R1; N3-R3; N4-F2].

- **Methodological differences** are clear. Hospitals use different approaches, including bottom-up and top-down methods, cost-based approaches, and financial-data-based calculation methods [N3-R1; N6-R1].
- **Scope differences** matter. Scope 3 emissions dominate, but they are harder to measure and report than Scope 1 and 2 emissions [N2-F1; N3-R3].
- **Data availability** is limited. The systematic review found severe reporting gaps, and only a small subset of hospitals had reports available [N2-F1; N2-R5]. One study also notes that its dataset is not publicly available due to ethical constraints [N5-F3].

**Confounding factors** are therefore important. Hospital size, location, and patient volume likely affect measurement effort and reporting completeness, but the evidence does not quantify these differences by ownership type [N2-F1; N3-R3; N4-F2]. The evidence also notes that the systematic review validated its search strategy by scanning websites of all hospitals in one federal state, suggesting that geographic scope matters [N2-F1].

The cluster analysis on climate protection strategies is limited to hospital administrative leaders and does not provide a direct ownership-type comparison [N5-F3]. So any observed differences would need to be interpreted cautiously [N2-F1; N2-R5; N4-F2].

### 5) Overall status of GHG reporting in German hospitals and practical implications

The overall status is **weak**. In 2020, GHG emission reports were available for only 12% of German hospitals [N2-R5]. No legal obligation exists for hospitals to report GHG emissions [N2-R2]. The systematic review also found severe gaps and noted that reports tend to focus on low-hanging fruits [N2-F1]. This means reporting is not widespread, not comprehensive, and not aligned with the full scope of emissions [N2-F1].

**Major gaps and barriers** include:
- No legal obligation [N2-R2].
- Low reporting rate and limited scope of reports [N2-R5; N2-F1].
- Dominance of scope 3 emissions, which are harder to measure [N2-F1; N3-R3].
- Methodological variation and limited access to standardized tools [N3-R1; N6-R1; N4-F2].

**Practical implications** are significant for policy and hospital management:
- **Policy implications** include the need for stronger incentives, standardized reporting frameworks, and possibly legal or voluntary requirements to improve coverage [N2-F1; N4-F2].
- **Hospital management implications** include the need for leadership engagement, better measurement tools, and greater attention to scope 3 emissions [N5-F3; N3-R3].
- The evidence also implies that hospitals may benefit from organizational strategies that align climate goals with operational leadership and employee engagement [N5-F3].

### 6) Bottom line

**The answer is not that ownership type explains a clear difference in reporting rates.** The evidence suggests instead that:
